newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African mining houses to spend $100m in Africa.
newsitem.headline: S.African mining houses to spend $100m in Africa.

text.p: South African mining houses could invest more than $100 million in mining projects in Africa this year, attracted by vast untapped geological potential.

Fleming Martin Securities mining research director Dennis Tucker told the Investing in Africa mining conference on Wednesday that difficult conditions in South Africa had prompted the companies to gradually increase their investments elsewhere in Africa.

Randgold and Exploration Company Ltd had acquired extensive mineral interests in west, central and east Africa covering 18,000 square kilometres as well as 15,000 square kilometres in South Africa and Namibia.
The group had 217 projects, including one operating mine, Mali's Syama, which provided a base of 200,000 ounces a year and a reserve of about 2.2 million ounces.
The attributable resource base had risen steadily over the past four years to around 5.8 million ounces with 3.8 million ounces in the measured and indicated category and the rest inferred.
"Over the next year we expect at least one bankable million ounce deposit in Mali," Tucker said.
"Randgold's activity will accelerate over the year as cash from the listing of Randgold Resources is injected into the company's very aggressive programme."
Randgold Resources had budgeted $15 million for exploration, most of which was for east and west Africa, particularly Mali, Burkino Faso and Tanzania.

Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd would spend about $45 million in Africa in 1996/97 compared to $100,000 in 1991. Most of this would be for grass roots expenditure with about two thirds concentrated in gold. About 80 geotechnicians and 600 support staff were involved in exploration.
Anglo's focus varied from Namibia to Mali and the project spread was broad with the Sadiola mine in Mali, managed on behalf of partner Iamgold, producing its first gold in early 1997.
"This is likely to be a 400,000 per annum producer with more potential currently under investigation," Tucker said.

JCL Ltd favoured using joint venture partners where possible. It was actively pursuing Lega Dembi in Ethiopia and had Prestea mine in Ghana, where a "decent resource both underground and surface is in the process of being delineated," he said.

The company had 37 prospects in seven countries and was examining opportunities in 19 other countries. Eighty-five percent of JCL's drive was focused on gold which generated 1.7 million new resource ounces in 1996.
"Base metals are not being ignored with interesting prospects in the eastern and western shores of Africa under the spotlight at present," Tucker said.
Net exploration expenditure in 1996 was $13 million "and this is expected to double in 1997," Tucker said.
Gencor Ltd was most active in Ghana, Ivory Coast and Burkino Faso while activities were likely to grow in Zambia and Mozambique.
"Gencor's exploration budget of $43 million in 1997 should see around 30 percent spent in Africa," Tucker said.
Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd had mainly concentrated on Ghana, where it controlled the Tarkwa underground mine which produced about 50,000 ounces a year.
"A bankable feasibility study on part of the 13 million ounce surface deposit has been completed," Tucker said.
-- Lynda Loxton, Cape Town newsroom, +27-21 25-2238
